sources.citation: Rice, Chris & Amy Rice. 2010. Finongan Organised Phonology Data. Ukarumpa: SIL-PNG. 12 pp. [Finongan fag / fino1238, which lists Mama among its major villages]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: For FINONGAN, not Mamaa: p. 6 Suprasegmentals 'Contrasting tones or tone patterns are not in evidence. Stress is unpredictable but non-contrastive. Closed syllables and syllables with lengthened vowels are often but not always stressed.' Relevant only as the language Mamaa speakers are shifting to.

sources.note: Nothing. Sociolinguistic rationale only (1997: 75% lexical similarity with Finongan; Mamaa villagers 'reported that they used to speak a different language'); cites Troolin & VanderWal 1997 unpublished Finongan preallocation survey.

sources.citation: McElhanon, Kenneth A. 1973. Towards a typology of the Finisterre-Huon languages, New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics B-22. Canberra: ANU. viii+80 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.harvard_location: Divinity School Library (offsite storage), call number - Ask at Circulation (Pamph. folio) BS 354 .Z91
sources.note: Mamaa appears only in the Erap family member list (p. vi). Phonology ch. 1 (pp. 5-8) covers ten representative languages (Uri for Erap) and has no stress/accent statement at all.

sources.citation: Claassen, Oren R. & Kenneth A. McElhanon. 1970. Languages of the Finisterre Range - New Guinea. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 11, Pacific Linguistics A-23: 45-78. Canberra: ANU.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Mamaa entry sec. 2.7.1 (pp. 56-57) is population/lexicostatistics only (pop. 200, 46% with Finungwan, being assimilated, mostly bilingual). Phonology sec. 6.1 (pp. 63-67) uses Uri as the Erap representative; its only stress sentence (p. 67): 'Stress is phonemic in Rawa but probably sub-phonemic in Yupna and Wantoat. In none of these languages does it carry a heavy functional load.. In Suroi stress is contrastive, but only on a limited number of words.' Nothing on Mamaa or Erap stress.

sources.citation: Hooley, Bruce A. & Kenneth A. McElhanon. 1970. Languages of the Morobe District - New Guinea. In S. A. Wurm & D. C. Laycock (eds), Pacific linguistic studies in honour of Arthur Capell, Pacific Linguistics C-13: 1065-1094. Canberra: ANU.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Mamaa p. 1073: 'a small language of one village on the banks of the lower Irumu River. The Mamaa speakers are gradually being assimilated by the Finungwan people and most of them are bilingual'; checklist no. 33 (pop. 200). Classification/lexicostatistics only.
